banner: Research context for analyst review — not a trading instruction.

input.raw_text: Yesterday May WTI settled at minus $37 a barrel — negative, a first in history — and the equity market barely flinched. The S&P has rallied hard off the March lows, the Nasdaq has clawed back to positive for the year, and the tapes tell two different stories. The oil collapse is largely plumbing: the May contract expired with Cushing storage nearly full, longs had nowhere to roll in a vicious contango, and index-ETF mechanics amplified the squeeze. June crude trades back in the twenties, a wide premium that says the dislocation was expiry arithmetic as much as demand. Meanwhile stimulus checks are landing, reopening chatter grows louder by the day, and equities are pricing the other side of the shutdown, storage tanks notwithstanding.
input.summary: May WTI's unprecedented negative settlement reflected an expiring contract, scarce Cushing storage, steep contango, and index-fund mechanics amid weak demand, while June crude remained above zero in the twenties. Equities showed limited reaction to the oil disruption, with the S&P rebounding sharply from March lows and the Nasdaq recovering to positive territory for the year as stimulus payments and reopening expectations supported optimism beyond the shutdown.

observations.statement: Unprecedented negative settlement in May WTI
Near-capacity Cushing storage around May expiry
Expiry pressure amplified by contango and index-fund mechanics
June crude priced in the twenties above the expiring May contract
Limited equity reaction to the oil-market disruption
Sharp S&P recovery from March lows
Nasdaq recovery into positive year-to-date territory
Growing optimism tied to stimulus payments and reopening expectations
Uncertain balance between technical oil dislocation and underlying demand weakness
